notes.body:
Kinship and oneness are two points on the same road, and these sayings about Maulana Ali walk us from one to the other. Kinship means **a closeness held across a distance** — two souls that resemble and are drawn to one another, the way a child carries a parent's likeness yet stays a separate person. That is what the passage first grants every believer: a felt nearness to the prophetic nature, sensed faintly at the core of one's own soul.

Oneness is what happens when that distance finally closes. When the Prophet places Maulana Ali at the very self (نفس) that speaks, he does not say Ali is *near* his soul or *like* his soul —

عليٌّ مِنِّي بِمَنْزِلَةِ نَفْسِي  
"Ali is to me at the station of my own self."

And when he says the belonging runs both ways at once —

أنْتَ مِنِّی وَ أَنَا مِنْکَ  
"You are from me, and I am from you,"

**neither can be pointed to without the other**, the way a flame lit from a flame becomes one light in which no seam can be found.

Why should words spoken of one man reach every sanctified soul? Because Maulana Ali stands here not as an exception to human nature but as its full flowering. What the ordinary believer feels as a faint kinship, he lived out to completion, so his oneness with the Prophet becomes **a promise** — the furthest reach of the very closeness already stirring, in some small measure, in us.

The road, then, has two stages we can name plainly:

1. Kinship — a resemblance and a pull across a gap that still remains.
2. Oneness — that gap dissolved, so that the soul and the prophetic nature are no longer two.

The Quran already whispers this second stage when it calls the Prophet nearer to the believers than they are to themselves —

ٱلنَّبِىُّ أَوْلَىٰ بِٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ مِنْ أَنفُسِهِمْ  
"The Prophet is closer to the believers than they are to themselves."  
Al-Ahzab 33:6

A closeness nearer to us than our own self is no longer a kinship standing beside us; it has become one with the ground of who we are.

etymology: نفس (self): from the root ن-ف-س, tied to breath and the breath of life — from it come تنفّس (to breathe) and نفيس (precious, dear). The نفس is the living core that breathes, so to be placed at another's نفس is to share one and the same breath of life, not merely to stand close to it.

منزلة (station): from the root ن-ز-ل, to descend, alight, and lodge. A منزلة is the very place where one comes down and settles, hence a standing or rank. To be بمنزلة نفسي is to occupy the same resting-place the Prophet's own self occupies — not a spot nearby, but his place.

أولى (closer, more entitled): from the root و-ل-ي, nearness with nothing set between — the same root that gives وليّ (guardian, near friend) and وِلاية (guardianship). As a comparative it means nearer-than, so calling the Prophet أولى to the believers than their own selves names a closeness with no gap left inside it.

It is a beautiful and important question to ask how we can understand Maulana Ali's influence. The key is to see the difference between building a house and planting a seed. While his role in formally constructing the 'house' of each science—with all its rules and defined structures—is a matter of historical discussion, his role as the one who planted the foundational 'seeds' is affirmed by the masters who came later. His teachings and personal example provided the **first creative impulse** for these fields of knowledge.

Imagine a powerful spring of fresh water bubbling up from the ground. Over time, people come and dig channels from that spring to water different gardens. One person might create an intricate system for a rose garden, another for a vegetable patch, and a third for an orchard. The gardeners are the later masters who developed the specific sciences like jurisprudence (فقہ), theology (كلام), and grammar (نحو). They did the work of structuring the disciplines, but they all drew their water from the same original, life-giving spring.

When masters from so many different fields—fields as diverse as law, rhetoric, and mysticism—all point back to the same source, it tells us something profound. This isn't simply a case of showing respect for a revered figure after the fact. It is a widespread testimony, from across different schools of thought, that the essential ideas, the spiritual and intellectual energy that gave birth to their disciplines, flowed from him. His sermons, his wisdom, and his way of uniting the inward spirit with the outward intellect created a powerful "radiance" that illuminated the path for generations of thinkers who would formalize these sciences.

Therefore, the later masters looking back to him is not a projection; it is an acknowledgement of their origin. They recognized that while they may have built the specific structures of their sciences, the very ground on which they built, and the spiritual and intellectual nourishment they relied upon, came from the wellspring of wisdom that was Maulana Ali.

***

فقہ (jurisprudence): From the root ف-ق-ه, which means to understand or to comprehend deeply. It signifies not just knowing a rule, but grasping its underlying wisdom and purpose. Thus, فقہ is the deep, intelligent understanding of divine law, connecting the outward regulation to its inner meaning and objective.
